summary: Defines the syntax used by the World-Wide Web to encode names and addresses of objects on the network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way of writing the name of anything on the Web so any computer can find it.

questions: what is the difference between a uri and a url
subtitle: The syntax the early World-Wide Web used to name and address any object on the network.

tldr.problem: The Web needs one way to name objects reachable through many different protocols and name spaces, and names and addresses cannot be converted the way data formats and protocols can.
tldr.mechanism: A URI is a scheme name, a colon, and a path whose format depends on the scheme. Characters outside a safe set are written as a percent sign plus two hex digits, and related URIs can be written in a shortened relative form.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents existing practice and is Informational. It does not specify an Internet standard, and the IESG note says a standard for general resource identifiers was under development.

sections.title: URIs, URLs and URNs
sections.content:
RFC 1630 defines the syntax the World-Wide Web initiative uses to encode the names and addresses of objects on the Internet. The web is meant to reach objects through an open-ended number of protocols, existing ones, ones invented for the web and ones yet to come.

A Universal Resource Identifier (URI) is a member of the universal set of names in registered name spaces and addresses referring to registered protocols or name spaces. A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is a form of URI that expresses an address which maps onto an access algorithm using network protocols. A Uniform Resource Name (URN) would be a more persistent name; the memo says that area is under discussion and is not addressed here.

The memo is written to document existing practice and give a reference point for URL and URN discussions. It states that the URI syntax and URL forms have been in widespread use by World-Wide Web software since 1990.
sections.plainLanguage: A URI is a name or address for anything on the network. Some are like street addresses (URLs), and some are meant to be names that never change (URNs).

sections.title: Why One Universal Syntax
sections.content:
Protocols can be bridged by gateways and data formats by conversion programs, but names and addresses cannot be converted in practice. They get passed on in many ways, from the backs of envelopes to hypertext objects, and may live a long time. So the memo defines a way to wrap a name from any registered name space and label it with that name space.

The syntax was designed to be extensible (new schemes can be added), complete (any naming scheme can be encoded) and printable (any URI can be expressed in 7-bit ASCII, even on paper). Extensibility comes from an arbitrary but registered prefix, read left to right, with a colon separating it from the rest. Completeness for binary names comes from encoding them in base 16 or 64.

The syntax says nothing about the properties of names in each name space. Those follow from each scheme's own specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone wanted to link to things in many different systems. Names are hard to convert later, so the idea was to give every name a label saying which system it belongs to.

sections.title: URI Syntax and Reserved Characters
sections.content:
A complete URI is a scheme, a colon, and a path whose format is a function of the scheme. Slashes in the path must imply a hierarchy. Several characters are reserved:

  • The percent sign (%) is the escape character and is never allowed for anything else.
  • The slash (/) separates hierarchical parts, and the segments . and .. are reserved too.
  • The hash sign separates the URI from a fragment identifier.
  • The question mark (?) separates a queryable object from a query, and inside the query the plus sign is shorthand for a space.
  • The asterisk and exclamation mark are reserved for special meaning within specific schemes.

The memo warns that a URI is not a filename, even though hierarchical paths look like unix filenames. A fragment identifier names part of an object, with syntax and meaning defined by the application or the content type. It does not imply the fragment can be extracted as an object in its own right.
sections.plainLanguage: A web address has a few special punctuation marks that each do a job, like marking where the name starts, where the folders are, and where a question begins.

sections.title: Percent Encoding
sections.content:
Characters that are not allowed, such as spaces, control characters and 8-bit characters beyond DEL (7F hex) of ISO Latin-1, are written as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits giving the ISO Latin 1 code. The percent sign was chosen over the backslash because shells interpret backslashes, and over the equals sign because that is used in attribute=value names.

The same method can make a URI safer or less strict by encoding or decoding additional characters, so two URIs must be brought to the same encoding level before they are compared. The reserved characters may never be encoded and unencoded this way, because they mean something different when encoded. A real percent sign must always be encoded, and a percent sign not followed by two hex characters is reserved for future extension.

The memo's examples show the effect: marie-claude and marie%2Dclaude are identical, but an encoded slash (%2F) has no hierarchical meaning, so that URI is not identical.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter or symbol might get mangled in the mail, you write it as a percent sign and a short code instead. Everyone can turn the code back into the original character.

sections.title: Partial (Relative) Forms
sections.content:
Inside an object whose URI is well defined, another URI can be given in abbreviated form where parts are the same as the context URI. That saves space and lets a group of objects move without changing every reference. Outside a well controlled context the full form must always be used.

A partial form is told apart from an absolute one because an absolute URI has a colon that comes before any slash. The rules are: if the schemes differ, give the whole absolute URI. Otherwise omit the scheme, and either borrow the start of the context URI up to a matching run of slashes, or drop the last path part of the context and append the partial URI. Then remove path elements of the form xxx/../ and /..

The memo also notes that gopher allowed unescaped slashes as data, so relative forms may not work for documents served by gopher servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a book you can say see the next chapter instead of the whole library address. A partial URI works the same way, relative to the page it appears on.

sections.title: Schemes and Registration
sections.content:
The memo lists schemes used by the Web at the time: http, ftp, gopher, mailto, news, telnet (with rlogin and tn3270), wais and file. It also proposes mid and cid for mail message and MIME body-part identifiers, not yet implemented to the author's knowledge. Others, such as X.500, Whois++ and network management databases, are left for study. The prefix urn: is reserved for the future URN standard.

A few scheme details follow from the text. For HTTP, the path is opaque to the client, and a fragment (the hash sign and what follows) is never sent to the server. An FTP URL defaults to anonymous login, and the data type can be given with a ;type= suffix. A file URL should carry a host part, where localhost or an empty host means the machine you are on.

A new scheme is introduced by mapping it onto the URL syntax with a new prefix. Experimental prefixes must start with x-. The memo proposes the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as registrar, and a submission must define an algorithm for retrieving any object in the scheme. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of address starts with a short label like http or mailto that says which system to use. New labels can be added, and there is a plan for one office to keep the list.

items.label: Escape

items.label: Hierarchy
items.desc: Separates path parts; the left part is closer to the root.

items.label: Fragment
items.desc: Separates the URI of an object from a fragment identifier.

items.label: Query
items.desc: Separates a queryable object from the query words.

items.desc: Shorthand for a space within a query string.

data.title: Generic URI syntax
data.code:
fragmentaddress   uri [ # fragmentid ]
uri               scheme : path [ ? search ]
scheme            ialpha
path              void | xpalphas [ / path ]
search            xalphas [ + search ]
fragmentid        xalphas
